dimension: Scheduling and resource-allocation theory for heterogeneous machines
summary:
The founder's problem is the classical R||Cmax problem — n jobs, m machines, a job-dependent processing time p_ij, minimise makespan — which is exactly "unrelated machines", the case where capability is a model-by-task-type matrix rather than one number per model. That problem has been studied continuously since 1990 and the field already contains direct, quantitative answers to both of his questions.

On "measure first or assign adaptively", the literature gives a sharp three-part answer. (1) Assigning with no capability information at all is provably bad: any speed-oblivious online algorithm has competitive ratio at least Omega(m), even if it knows every job's size, even on uniform-speed machines (Lindermayr, Megow, Rapp, ICML 2023, Observation 1.1). So his mechanism 2, taken literally as a routing policy, is the worst case in the theory. (2) But the information needed is far less than he assumes. Knowing only a global ORDER of machines, with no magnitudes at all, buys 8-competitive clairvoyant scheduling and 216-competitive non-clairvoyant scheduling on related machines, and Theta(log min{n,m}) on unrelated machines (same paper, Theorems 1.3 and 1.4). A knockout bracket produces exactly an order. That is the sufficient statistic. (3) The entire value of knowing speeds in advance is bounded. In speed-robust scheduling you must commit jobs to m bags before any speed is revealed, and the best achievable robustness factor is 2 - 1/m in general and tight at e/(e-1), about 1.58, when bags equal machines (Eberle, Hoeksma, Megow, Noelke, Schewior, Simon, IPCO 2021 / Math. Prog. 197, 2023). So a perfect cold-start measurement can recover at most about 58% to 100% in makespan — before subtracting what the measurement itself costs.

Two further results bind hard. Migration is necessary: any non-migratory speed-oblivious algorithm is Omega(m)-competitive even when the order is known (Lindermayr et al., Theorem 3.1), so a tier assigned once per experiment cannot be constant-competitive. And greedily routing to the best-measured machine — his "promote to top tier" — has unbounded competitive ratio, Omega(n) (same paper, Appendix C, "Iterative Greedy").
is_the_wheel_already_invented: Yes, substantially. The scheduling problem he describes is R||Cmax (makespan on unrelated parallel machines), open since Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos, Mathematical Programming 46:259-271, 1990. His cold-start probe is computerized adaptive testing (item response theory, maximum Fisher information item selection) applied to machines instead of people, and it has already been applied to language-model evaluation. His knockout bracket is the "speed-ordered machines" model of Lindermayr, Megow and Rapp (ICML 2023), which exists precisely because somebody asked his question and proved what an order alone is worth. His "commit before you know capability" variant is speed-robust scheduling (Eberle et al., IPCO 2021). His no-central-server constraint is Condor matchmaking with ClassAds (Raman, Livny, Solomon, HPDC 1998) and Sparrow (Ousterhout, Wendell, Zaharia, Stoica, SOSP 2013). His "never set a model aside, reassign it" is BOINC adaptive replication plus per-(host, application-version) reputation (Anderson, "BOINC: A Platform for Volunteer Computing", arXiv:1903.01699). What is NOT invented: nobody has solved the combined problem of paying a per-probe cost to learn individual entries of an m-by-n unrelated-speed matrix and then scheduling against it. Pandora's box and scheduling-with-testing price the probe but only for job processing times, not for a machine-by-job capability matrix. That specific gap is where CDSFL has something genuinely new to contribute.

mechanisms.name: Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos LP rounding for R||Cmax
mechanisms.what_it_does: Binary-searches a target makespan T and rounds an extreme point of the assignment LP to an integral schedule of makespan at most 2T, for arbitrary job-dependent processing times p_ij. Still the best known general worst-case ratio after 35 years; no polynomial algorithm can beat 3/2 unless P = NP. A (2 - 1/m) refinement is attributed to Shchepin and Vakhania.
mechanisms.citation: J. K. Lenstra, D. B. Shmoys, E. Tardos, "Approximation algorithms for scheduling unrelated parallel machines", Mathematical Programming 46:259-271, 1990. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01585745
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Does not. It is offline and assumes the full p_ij matrix is already known. It is the TARGET that any cold-start measurement exists to serve, not a cold-start mechanism.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Directly and completely. 'Unrelated machines' is the strongest heterogeneity model in the field: every machine-job pair gets its own processing time, so a desktop that is good at one task and hopeless at another is representable with no loss.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the right formalisation of the objective. It transfers as the offline benchmark against which any CDSFL allocator should be measured. What breaks if adopted naively: it needs the whole matrix, it is a one-shot assignment, and the 3/2 hardness means no amount of measurement precision gets below 1.5 in the worst case. Do not promise better than a factor 2 from any allocator in this model.

mechanisms.name: Speed-oblivious lower bound (Omega(m))
mechanisms.what_it_does: Proves that an algorithm that does not know the processing speeds has competitive ratio at least Omega(m) for total (weighted) completion time on m machines, even if it is clairvoyant (knows every job's size) and even if machines are merely related (one speed scalar each). The adversary simply accelerates whichever machine the algorithm tries last.
mechanisms.citation: A. Lindermayr, N. Megow, M. Rapp, "Speed-Oblivious Online Scheduling: Knowing (Precise) Speeds is not Necessary", ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Observation 1.1. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lindermayr23a/lindermayr23a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the impossibility theorem for cold start. With 0 capability information and adversarial inputs, you lose a factor linear in roster size. With 700 models that is catastrophic.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The bound is proved in the easier 'related machines' case, so it holds a fortiori for job-dependent capability.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the direct answer to 'assume NO capability at the outset'. Transfers as a hard constraint: some capability signal is mandatory. It does NOT say the signal must be a measured magnitude — see the speed-ordered result next. What breaks: mechanism 2 used as a routing policy rather than as a measurement procedure.

mechanisms.name: Speed-ordered machines (order without magnitudes)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Assumes only that a single global ordering of machines by unknown speed is known. Gives a clairvoyant algorithm that is at most 8-competitive on speed-ordered related machines (Theorem 1.3) and a non-clairvoyant algorithm that is at most 216-competitive on related machines and Theta(log min{n, m})-competitive on unrelated machines (Theorem 1.4). The Omega(m) bound collapses because the machines become distinguishable.
mechanisms.citation: A. Lindermayr, N. Megow, M. Rapp, ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Theorems 1.3 and 1.4. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lindermayr23a/lindermayr23a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It minimises what cold start must produce. You do not need speeds, costs, or a calibrated score. An ordinal ranking is enough for constant-competitive scheduling.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Partly. The model presumes ONE order valid for all jobs. Genuinely unrelated capability (one model better at algebra, another at combinatorics) has no such order, and that case falls back to Omega(m).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This vindicates the knockout bracket, and it is the single most useful result for CDSFL: a tournament whose only output is a total order is provably sufficient, which removes the need to calibrate difficulty, cost and time into one comparable number. What breaks: if capability is genuinely non-transitive across claim types, a single bracket produces a meaningless order. Run one bracket per claim class, or accept the Omega(m) regime.

mechanisms.name: Migration-necessity theorem
mechanisms.what_it_does: Any NON-MIGRATORY speed-oblivious algorithm has competitive ratio at least Omega(m) for total completion time on m machines, even if it is clairvoyant, the machines are related, and the speed order is known. Work must be movable between machines after assignment.
mechanisms.citation: A. Lindermayr, N. Megow, M. Rapp, ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Theorem 3.1 (proof in Appendix B). https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lindermayr23a/lindermayr23a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Shows cold-start measurement is not enough on its own. Even a perfect order does not rescue a one-shot assignment.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Holds on related machines, so it is not an artefact of job-dependent speed.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as a design constraint that contradicts static tiering: a tier fixed at the start of an experiment is a non-migratory assignment and is provably Omega(m). The founder's 'reassigned, not deleted' instinct is correct and must be enforced per claim, not per experiment. What breaks: any scheme where a demoted model cannot pick up a claim that the top tier is stuck on.

mechanisms.name: Iterative Greedy is not competitive
mechanisms.what_it_does: The policy 'at any time, assign the alive job j to the free machine i with the largest estimated speed s_ij' is shown to have competitive ratio at least Omega(n), i.e. unbounded in the number of jobs.
mechanisms.citation: A. Lindermayr, N. Megow, M. Rapp, ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Appendix C ("We show in Appendix C that Iterative Greedy is not competitive (lower bound of Omega(n))"). https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lindermayr23a/lindermayr23a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Irrelevant; it fails even with perfect speed knowledge.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is the natural heterogeneity-aware greedy rule, and it is exactly what fails.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the sharpest falsification of 'promote the top performers to the top tier' and then route work there. Greedy best-machine routing is the policy with the worst proven guarantee in the whole set. Interestingly the same paper's EMPIRICAL section finds Iterative Greedy performs best among non-clairvoyant heuristics on real hardware, so the failure is worst-case, not average-case. Transfers as: if CDSFL uses best-measured routing, it must be bounded by a fairness or occupancy constraint, and it cannot carry a worst-case claim.

mechanisms.name: Speed-robust scheduling (commit before speeds are revealed)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Jobs must be partitioned into at most m bags with machine speeds entirely unknown; speeds are then revealed and whole bags are assigned to machines. Robustness factor 2 - 1/m in general, with tight bounds for every m when the number of bags equals the number of machines, approaching e/(e-1), about 1.58, for large m. A later paper generalises the e/(e-1) bound to any number of bags b >= m and improves the previous 1.8.
mechanisms.citation: F. Eberle, R. Hoeksma, N. Megow, L. Noelke, K. Schewior, B. Simon, "Speed-Robust Scheduling: Sand, Bricks, and Rocks", IPCO 2021; Mathematical Programming 197(2):1009-1048, 2023. arXiv:2011.05181. Follow-up: J. Minarik, "Speed-robust scheduling revisited", arXiv:2407.11670.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It IS the zero-information case, solved. You can commit work to groups knowing nothing about capability and lose at most a factor of about 1.58 to 2.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Handles arbitrary unknown machine speeds, revealed adversarially after commitment.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the number that prices the founder's cold-start tournament. The maximum possible payoff from perfect advance capability knowledge, in makespan, is bounded by about 1.58 to 2. If the probing tournament consumes more than roughly 37% of the experiment's budget it is net negative by construction. What breaks: nothing in CDSFL breaks; what breaks is the case for an elaborate probe.

mechanisms.name: Scheduling with speed predictions (robustness-consistency trade-off)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Machine speeds are unknown but predicted with multiplicative error eta >= 1. Gives an approximation of min{eta^2 (1 + alpha), 2 + 2/alpha} for any alpha in (0,1): near-optimal when predictions are accurate, and never worse than 2 + 2/alpha even when predictions are arbitrarily wrong.
mechanisms.citation: E. Balkanski, T. Ou, C. Stein, H.-T. Wei, "Scheduling with Speed Predictions", arXiv:2205.01247 (2022); WAOA 2023, LNCS 14297:74-89; Theory of Computing Systems 69, article 16, 2025.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Treats the cold-start measurement as an untrusted prediction rather than ground truth, and degrades gracefully. alpha is a tunable dial on how much to trust it.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Predicts per-machine speeds; the eta^2 term is the price of error.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the correct contract for a measured capability estimate: use it, but cap the damage. Transfers directly as the design pattern for CDSFL's capability store. Note the eta^2: prediction error is SQUARED in the guarantee, so a sloppy cold-start probe is worse than a crude one that is honest about its uncertainty.

mechanisms.name: Distortion-error bounds for speed predictions (8mu / 7.216mu^2 / 108mu)
mechanisms.what_it_does: With predicted speeds s_hat_ij and distortion error mu = mu_1 * mu_2 (worst over-estimate times worst under-estimate), gives algorithms that are 8mu-competitive clairvoyant, 7.216mu^2-competitive clairvoyant and non-preemptive, and 108mu-competitive non-clairvoyant, for total weighted completion time on unrelated machines. A ratio linear in mu is proved best possible, even for migratory algorithms on related machines.
mechanisms.citation: A. Lindermayr, N. Megow, M. Rapp, ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 2.7. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lindermayr23a/lindermayr23a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Prices the cold start exactly. Measurement error enters the guarantee linearly if you may preempt and migrate, and QUADRATICALLY if you may not.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Full job-dependent speeds, which is CDSFL's case.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The most actionable single inequality for CDSFL: the cost of a stale capability table is linear in its distortion if claims can be re-dispatched mid-flight, and quadratic if each claim is irrevocably bound to one model. That is an independent, quantitative argument for making CDSFL assignments preemptible. The paper's own experiments add: when predictions are inaccurate, relying on the ORDER beats relying on the magnitudes.

mechanisms.name: HEFT and CPOP
mechanisms.what_it_does: HEFT ranks tasks by upward rank on a DAG and assigns each to the processor minimising its earliest finish time, using insertion into idle slots. CPOP prioritises by the sum of upward and downward ranks and pins the whole critical path to the single processor that minimises its total execution time. Both take an estimated computation-cost matrix w[task][processor] plus communication costs.
mechanisms.citation: H. Topcuoglu, S. Hariri, M.-Y. Wu, "Performance-Effective and Low-Complexity Task Scheduling for Heterogeneous Computing", IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 13(3):260-274, 2002, DOI 10.1109/71.993206.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not. The cost matrix is an input. In practice it is populated from prior runs or from a profiling pass, which is precisely the gap the founder is trying to fill.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is its reason for existing: per-processor, per-task cost, with communication costs between differently-located processors.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: If CDSFL has dependencies between claims (a falsifier that must wait for a proof), HEFT is the standard engineering default and should be the baseline any CDSFL allocator is compared against. It has no worst-case guarantee, only extensive empirical evidence. What breaks: HEFT assumes a single fixed cost matrix, so it inherits the eta^2 sensitivity above.

mechanisms.name: Graham list scheduling (2 - 1/m) and LPT (4/3 - 1/(3m)); timing anomalies
mechanisms.what_it_does: Any list schedule on m identical machines is within 2 - 1/m of optimal; sorting the list longest-first gives 4/3 - 1/(3m), and both bounds are tight. Graham's companion result is that adding a machine, shortening every job, or removing a precedence constraint can each INCREASE the makespan.
mechanisms.citation: R. L. Graham, "Bounds for Certain Multiprocessing Anomalies", Bell System Technical Journal 45(9):1563-1581, 1966; "Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies", SIAM J. Applied Mathematics 17(2):416-429, 1969.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Needs nothing at all: a machine that becomes free takes the next item off the list. The measurement-free baseline is already within a factor 2 on identical machines.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It does not. The 2 - 1/m bound is for identical machines. On uniform (single-speed-scalar) machines the adapted LPT rule is at most 2, with worst case shown to lie in (1.52, 1.67).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the sanity floor: measure nothing, let any free model grab the next claim, and on homogeneous capability you are within a factor 2. The anomaly result transfers as a direct warning on the founder's 'roster of 1, 5, 6, 70 or 700 without redesign' requirement: adding models to a list-scheduled system can make it finish LATER, so roster growth must be tested, not assumed monotone. Uniform-machine LPT citation: T. Gonzalez, O. H. Ibarra, S. Sahni, "Bounds for LPT Schedules on Uniform Processors", SIAM J. Computing 6(1):155-166, 1977; interval (1.52, 1.67) due to Friesen.

mechanisms.name: Hochbaum-Shmoys dual approximation PTAS for uniform machines
mechanisms.what_it_does: Guesses a target makespan d, tests feasibility with a relaxed (1 + epsilon) decision procedure, and binary-searches. Yields a polynomial-time approximation scheme for Q||Cmax, i.e. any fixed ratio 1 + epsilon, when each machine has a single speed scalar.
mechanisms.citation: D. S. Hochbaum, D. B. Shmoys, "A polynomial approximation scheme for scheduling on uniform processors: using the dual approximation approach", SIAM J. Computing 17(3):539-551, 1988.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Requires the speed scalars.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Handles machines of arbitrarily different speed, but only if the speed ratio is the SAME for every job.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The contrast with R||Cmax is the useful content. If CDSFL can justify collapsing capability to one scalar per model, the problem becomes approximable to any accuracy. If capability is genuinely job-dependent, you are capped at 2 and no measurement effort moves that. So the highest-value question for CDSFL is not 'how do we measure capability' but 'is capability one number per model or a matrix'. That is empirically testable on the existing seat archive.

mechanisms.name: Work stealing (Blumofe-Leiserson)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Idle workers steal work at random from other workers' deques. For fully strict computations, expected execution time is O(T_1/P + T_infinity) where T_1 is the work and T_infinity the critical path; space at most S_1 * P; all three bounds existentially optimal to within a constant factor.
mechanisms.citation: R. D. Blumofe, C. E. Leiserson, "Scheduling multithreaded computations by work stealing", FOCS 1994, pp. 356-368; Journal of the ACM 46(5):720-748, 1999, DOI 10.1145/324133.324234.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Needs zero capability information. A fast worker simply steals more often. Load balance is an emergent property of receiver-initiated pull, not of a measurement.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is where it needs care. Bender's dissertation notes that for heterogeneous processors the critical-path term divided by average speed is no longer a valid lower bound, and that even with unvarying speeds the best known approximation ratio for the heterogeneous DAG case is only O(log p).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the allocation MECHANISM that satisfies the founder's hardest constraints at once: no central server, scale-free from 1 to 700 participants, capability never named because it is never represented. A slow desktop among supercomputers simply steals fewer claims. What breaks: the clean O(T_1/P + T_infinity) guarantee does not survive heterogeneity, so CDSFL cannot cite it as a bound, only as a design. Reference for the heterogeneous caveat: M. A. Bender, "Scheduling DAGs on Asynchronous Processors" / dissertation, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~bender/newpub/BenderPh07.pdf

mechanisms.name: Bender-Rabin high-utilization scheduler and work mugging
mechanisms.what_it_does: Extends work stealing to processors of different speeds. Each processor maintains an estimate of its own speed; communication has a cost; all scheduling is online. Adds 'work mugging' / snatching, in which a fast processor takes work from a randomly chosen slower processor when it cannot steal any.
mechanisms.citation: M. A. Bender, M. O. Rabin, "Online Scheduling of Parallel Programs on Heterogeneous Systems with Applications to Cilk", Theory of Computing Systems 35(3):289-304, 2002, DOI 10.1007/s00224-002-1055-5; earlier as "Scheduling Cilk multithreaded parallel programs on processors of different speeds", SPAA 2000, pp. 13-21.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By self-measurement. Each node estimates its OWN speed locally; no global capability table and no central registry are ever built. That is the cheapest possible cold start and it is fully decentralised.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Designed for it, including the desktop-versus-supercomputer case: a fast node actively mugs work off slow nodes rather than waiting for them.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the closest published match to what the founder wants: measured capability, self-reported, continuously updated, no central authority, no model ever excluded, and work migrates from slow to fast. [VERIFY:current] I could not retrieve the paper's theorem statements from open sources; the exact bound should be read from the DOI before being quoted.

mechanisms.name: Power of two choices (balanced allocations)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Sampling d >= 2 bins at random and placing the ball in the less loaded one reduces maximum load from about log n / log log n to log log n / log d + O(1). Going from 1 to 2 choices is an exponential improvement; going beyond 2 only improves by a constant factor.
mechanisms.citation: Y. Azar, A. Z. Broder, A. R. Karlin, E. Upfal, "Balanced Allocations", STOC 1994; SIAM J. Computing 29(1):180-200, 1999. M. Mitzenmacher, "The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing", IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 12(10):1094-1104, 2001.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Requires only an observable queue length, never a capability estimate. Works from the first ball.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Badly, unmodified. See the next entry.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the cheap decentralised primitive, and as a strong argument for small d: probing 2 candidates per claim captures almost all of the available benefit, so CDSFL should not probe the whole roster. What breaks: the bound is for identical bins.

mechanisms.name: Power-of-d loses stability on heterogeneous servers
mechanisms.what_it_does: With unequal service rates, randomly sampling d servers from the whole population shrinks the stability region, because the fast servers are sampled too rarely; the system can become unstable at arrival rates well below capacity when capacity is concentrated in a few fast servers. Stability is recovered by sampling within a randomly chosen server TYPE, by speed-aware query and routing, or by adding memory of past choices.
mechanisms.citation: A. Mukhopadhyay, R. R. Mazumdar, "Analysis of Randomized Join-the-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) Schemes in Large Heterogeneous Processor-Sharing Systems", IEEE Trans. Control of Network Systems; K. Gardner, J. A. Jaleel, A. Wickeham, S. Doroudi, "Scalable load balancing in the presence of heterogeneous servers", Performance Evaluation, 2020, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0166531620300717; X. Zhou, N. Shroff, A. Wierman, "Asymptotically optimal load balancing in large-scale heterogeneous systems with multiple dispatchers" / LSQ, arXiv:2003.02368.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the cold-start failure mode. Blind random sampling with heterogeneous capacity can deliver LESS throughput than the roster's actual capacity.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is the negative result about heterogeneity: the fix provably requires type or speed information.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the strongest quantitative objection to mechanism 2 as a steady-state policy. A roster where 2 or 3 models hold most of the useful capability and 60 hold little is exactly the regime where random pairing goes unstable. Transfers as: stratify by measured tier and sample WITHIN a tier, which is a hybrid of his two mechanisms and is the published fix.

mechanisms.name: Sparrow: decentralised scheduling with batch sampling and late binding
mechanisms.what_it_does: Stateless, decentralised schedulers with no global cluster view. For a job of m tasks it probes d*m random workers and places tasks on the least loaded, because plain power-of-two-choices degrades as job parallelism grows. Late binding defers the task-to-worker commitment until the worker is actually ready, cutting median response time by up to 45% over batch sampling alone. Reported 4x to 8x reduction in median query response time versus random assignment.
mechanisms.citation: K. Ousterhout, P. Wendell, M. Zaharia, I. Stoica, "Sparrow: Distributed, Low Latency Scheduling", SOSP 2013, pp. 69-84. https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p69-ousterhout.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No capability table at all; queue state is sampled per job.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Only through observed queue occupancy, and the paper itself notes queue length is a weak predictor of wait time, which is why late binding exists.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the founder's 'no central server beyond the endpoints' requirement, built and measured at scale. Late binding is the mechanism CDSFL most needs and is most likely to omit: do not bind a claim to a model until that model is free to start it. Transfers almost unchanged. What breaks: Sparrow has no competitive-ratio proof, only measurements, and it cannot express inter-job constraints.

mechanisms.name: Stale capability information degrades deterministic routing
mechanisms.what_it_does: In a model where each arriving task sees queue lengths as they were T seconds ago, sending tasks to the apparently least-loaded server significantly HURTS performance once the information is stale, unlike the fresh-information case; adding a small amount of randomness (choose the lighter of 2 random servers) restores performance close to perfect-information levels.
mechanisms.citation: M. Mitzenmacher, "How Useful Is Old Information?", PODC 1997, pp. 83-91; IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 11(1):6-20, 2000. https://www.eecs.harvard.edu/~michaelm/NEWWORK/postscripts/oldinfo-jver-submit.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Shows that a measurement's VALUE decays with age, and that acting deterministically on a decayed measurement is worse than acting randomly.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Model is homogeneous servers, so the result is about information staleness, not speed differences.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: A capability ranking fixed once at the start of an experiment is stale information, and this result says deterministic top-tier routing on stale information herds and self-defeats. Transfers as: always inject randomness into the routing even when a ranking exists. This is independent corroboration of the Iterative-Greedy failure from a completely different literature.

mechanisms.name: Non-clairvoyant scheduling with unknown job sizes
mechanisms.what_it_does: With job sizes unknown, round robin achieves competitive ratio 2 - 2/(n+1) for total completion time on one processor and this matches the deterministic lower bound; the ratio tends to 2. For total FLOW time the bounds are much worse: Omega(n^(1/3)) deterministic and Omega(log n) randomized.
mechanisms.citation: R. Motwani, S. Phillips, E. Torng, "Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling", SODA 1993; Theoretical Computer Science 130(1):17-47, 1994. https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.5555/313559.313845
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Needs nothing. Round robin, the policy that looks maximally wasteful, is provably the best deterministic policy when sizes are unknown.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Single machine / identical machines. Heterogeneity is handled by later work (Proportional Fairness, 128-competitive and improved to 108 for weighted completion time on unrelated machines).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as a correction to intuition: when claim difficulty is unknown, giving every model an equal slice is near-optimal for throughput, and the heterogeneous generalisation (Proportional Fairness) is a small constant. This is the published rival to the founder's tiering, and it needs no tournament. Reference for Proportional Fairness: S. Im, J. Kulkarni, K. Munagala, "Competitive Algorithms from Competitive Equilibria: Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling under Polyhedral Constraints", JACM 2018.

mechanisms.name: Resource augmentation: speed substitutes for information
mechanisms.what_it_does: Shows that simple online algorithms become constant-competitive for flow time and firm real-time scheduling if the online scheduler is given a slightly faster processor than the adversary, and reads this as a modest speed increase giving roughly the benefit of knowing job sizes in advance.
mechanisms.citation: B. Kalyanasundaram, K. Pruhs, "Speed is as powerful as clairvoyance", FOCS 1995, pp. 214-221; Journal of the ACM 47(4):617-643, 2000, DOI 10.1145/347476.347479.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By refusing to pay for it. Buy a little extra capacity instead of buying information.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Single-processor model; later multiprocessor flow-time results with epsilon resource augmentation extend it.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The cleanest economic argument against the founder's probe: spending the probe's token budget on extra capacity instead buys the same benefit as knowing what you were trying to measure. For CDSFL this is directly costable, because probe cost and extra-seat cost are both measured in tokens. Transfers as a budget comparison CDSFL should actually run.

mechanisms.name: Pandora's box and the price of information
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each option has a known value distribution and a known inspection cost. The optimal policy is an INDEX rule: compute each box's reservation value from its own distribution and cost, open in descending order, stop when the best realised value exceeds the highest reservation value among unopened boxes. Crucially, expected value is the WRONG index: a box with higher mean, lower cost and lower variance can have a lower reservation value and should be opened second.
mechanisms.citation: M. L. Weitzman, "Optimal Search for the Best Alternative", Econometrica 47(3):641-654, 1979. https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/weitzman/files/optimalsearchbestalternative.pdf ; generalisation to combinatorial objectives: S. Singla, "The Price of Information in Combinatorial Optimization", SODA 2018, pp. 2523-2532, arXiv:1711.00405.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the theory of whether and in what order to pay to measure. It gives the optimal stopping rule, which the founder's scheme lacks entirely: his recursion probes the whole roster regardless of what it has already learned.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Heterogeneous inspection costs and heterogeneous value distributions are first-class in the model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the correct framework for 'should I spend tokens testing this model'. It supplies the stopping rule: stop probing as soon as the best measured model beats every unprobed model's reservation value. What breaks: Weitzman's optimality needs INDEPENDENT distributions, and model capabilities are strongly correlated (shared training data, shared benchmarks), where index policies are only constant-factor approximate. Also fails if you may use a model without testing it, which CDSFL can.

mechanisms.name: Scheduling with testing / explorable uncertainty
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each job may be run untested at an upper-bound cost, or TESTED at a cost to reveal its true processing time and then run. For makespan the optimal deterministic competitive ratio is exactly the golden ratio phi, about 1.618, and the optimal randomized ratio is exactly 4/3; both are tight. Albers and Eckl extend both to non-uniform test times. For total completion time the best known deterministic ratio has come down to about 2.3165 and randomized to about 2.1523.
mechanisms.citation: C. Duerr, T. Erlebach, N. Megow, J. Meissner, "Scheduling with Explorable Uncertainty", ITCS 2018, LIPIcs 94:30:1-30:14; journal version "An Adversarial Model for Scheduling with Testing", Algorithmica, arXiv:1709.02592. S. Albers, A. Eckl, "Explorable Uncertainty in Scheduling with Non-Uniform Testing Times", WAOA 2020, arXiv:2009.13316.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Prices the test explicitly, which is what the founder's mechanism omits. The whole decision space between 'test everything' and 'test nothing' is bounded by phi for makespan.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Uncertainty is per JOB, not per machine, so this is the dual of the founder's problem; the multiprocessor variants (Albers-Eckl WADS 2021, latest ratio about 2.8681) move toward it.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the second independent bound on the payoff of probing: for makespan, no testing policy beats 1.618 and the best randomized one is 4/3. Combined with the 1.58 speed-robust bound, two separate literatures agree that the value of pre-measurement sits between about 1.3 and 2. That is the headline number the founder asked for.

mechanisms.name: Gittins index for unknown job sizes
mechanisms.what_it_does: When job sizes are unknown but drawn from a known distribution, the Gittins index policy, which prioritises by a function of the service a job has already received, minimises mean response time in the M/G/1 queue. The SOAP framework gives one response-time analysis for all age-based policies. Monotonic Gittins is heavy-traffic optimal in M/G/k and M-SERPT is a 2-approximation. Empirical Gittins builds the policy from samples when the distribution is unknown.
mechanisms.citation: Z. Scully, M. Harchol-Balter, A. Scheller-Wolf, "SOAP: One Clean Analysis of All Age-Based Scheduling Policies", SIGMETRICS 2018; Z. Scully, M. Harchol-Balter, "The Gittins Policy in the M/G/1 Queue", WiOpt 2021; Z. Scully, I. Grosof, M. Harchol-Balter, "Optimal Multiserver Scheduling with Unknown Job Sizes in Heavy Traffic", arXiv:2003.13232.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By using elapsed service as the only available evidence about a job, updated continuously. No pre-measurement phase.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Job-size heterogeneity, not machine heterogeneity. The multiserver extensions are the relevant direction.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The useful transfer is the shape of the answer: the optimal policy under uncertainty is an INDEX computed per unit of work from evidence accumulated so far, not a tier assigned in advance. If CDSFL wants an optimal allocator rather than a good one, this is the form it takes.

mechanisms.name: Queueing bandits with unknown service rates
mechanisms.what_it_does: Servers have unknown service rates learned only from observed departures. Queue-regret against an oracle that knows the rates grows logarithmically at first and then DECAYS roughly as 1/t, because regenerative cycles shorten as the algorithm learns. A companion dispatching paper notes that, unlike a classical bandit where exactly one arm is optimal, an optimal queueing policy typically uses SEVERAL fast servers.
mechanisms.citation: S. Krishnasamy, R. Sen, R. Johari, S. Shakkottai, "Learning Unknown Service Rates in Queues: A Multiarmed Bandit Approach", Operations Research 69(1):315-330, 2021, DOI 10.1287/opre.2020.1995, arXiv:1604.06377; T. Choudhury, G. Joshi, W. Wang, S. Shakkottai, "Job Dispatching Policies for Queueing Systems with Unknown Service Rates", ACM MobiHoc 2021, arXiv:2106.04707.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Learns rates while serving, with quantified regret, and the regret eventually shrinks rather than accumulating. This is the 'assign adaptively' answer with a bound attached.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Directly: unknown and unequal service rates are the model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Two transfers. First, you do not need a separate measurement phase at all: the cost of learning while working is bounded and eventually decays. Second, and against the founder's design, the optimal allocation spreads across SEVERAL fast servers rather than concentrating on one winner, because queueing makes the winner congest. That refutes a winner-take-all top tier on efficiency grounds, not just fairness grounds.

mechanisms.name: BOINC adaptive replication with per-(host, application-version) reputation
mechanisms.what_it_does: Every job is initially replicated on 2 unrelated hosts, at least halving usable capacity. The server then tracks, per (host, application-version) pair, the count N of consecutive jobs validated by replication; once N exceeds a threshold, replication becomes probabilistic with probability tending to 0 as N grows, moving the capacity factor back toward 1. Homogeneous redundancy sends further instances of a job only to numerically equivalent hosts. No two instances of a job go to hosts owned by the same volunteer.
mechanisms.citation: D. P. Anderson, "BOINC: A Platform for Volunteer Computing", Journal of Grid Computing 18:99-122, 2020, arXiv:1903.01699; "Celebrating Diversity in Volunteer Computing", HICSS 2008, https://boinc.berkeley.edu/boinc_papers/hicss_08/hicss_08.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Assume nothing, replicate everything, and decay the replication rate as evidence accumulates. This is a cold start that costs a factor of 2 up front and amortises to nearly free, with no tournament and no idle probing.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Reputation is per APPLICATION VERSION, not per host, explicitly because a machine can be reliable on one workload and unreliable on another. That is the unrelated-machines insight, implemented and deployed.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The closest deployed analogue to what the founder wants, across hundreds of thousands of untrusted heterogeneous machines with no shared trust: capability is measured, continuously re-measured, never a name, and no host is ever permanently excluded. Transfers nearly unchanged, with one hard caveat: BOINC establishes correctness by AGREEMENT between replicas, which CDSFL forbids under its no-model-voting rule. CDSFL would have to replace agreement with its own falsifier-based validation while keeping the decaying-replication accounting.

mechanisms.name: Condor matchmaking with ClassAds
mechanisms.what_it_does: Resources and jobs each publish a classified advertisement containing Requirements (a boolean constraint on the other party) and Rank (a preference expression). A matchmaker pairs them bilaterally; the claiming protocol then binds them. Extended to resource usage history, variable granularity, approximate matches, multilateral matchmaking and gangmatching for co-allocation.
mechanisms.citation: R. Raman, M. Livny, M. Solomon, "Matchmaking: Distributed Resource Management for High Throughput Computing", HPDC 1998 (7th IEEE Int. Symp. High Performance Distributed Computing), Chicago; "Matchmaking: An extensible framework for distributed resource management", Cluster Computing 2(2):129-138, 1999; D. Thain, T. Tannenbaum, M. Livny, "Distributed computing in practice: the Condor experience", Concurrency and Computation 17(2-4):323-356, 2005.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No global capability model is needed. Each side advertises what it has and what it needs, and matching is symmetric and local. New devices added to existing clusters are handled without redesign, which is the founder's 1-to-700 requirement.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is its purpose: arbitrarily different machines describe themselves in their own terms rather than being scored on a common scale.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the schema for the founder's peer-to-peer mode: a model advertises measured rates and constraints, a claim advertises its requirements and rank, and a matchmaker that holds no state pairs them. It removes the need for a central capability registry while keeping capability measured. What breaks: matchmaking gives no makespan guarantee and the original algorithm was cubic in the number of ads (later reduced to linear by Islam et al.).

mechanisms.name: LATE: progress-rate-based straggler speculation
mechanisms.what_it_does: Replaces 'compare each task's progress score with the average' by estimating each task's longest approximate time to end as (1 - ProgressScore)/ProgressRate, speculating the task with the latest estimated finish, launching the speculative copy on a FAST node, and capping total speculative tasks. Reported to finish jobs on average 58% faster than the default scheduler when stragglers are present, 27% faster with no faulty nodes, and up to 2x on 200 virtual machines.
mechanisms.citation: M. Zaharia, A. Konwinski, A. D. Joseph, R. Katz, I. Stoica, "Improving MapReduce Performance in Heterogeneous Environments", OSDI 2008, pp. 29-42. https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~matei/papers/2008/osdi_late.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Measures rate online from partial progress, with no prior capability model. Heterogeneity is discovered, not configured.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is the paper's entire subject: the default homogeneous heuristic causes severe degradation on heterogeneous hardware, and the fix is to use rate rather than absolute progress.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the operational pattern for a slow model: do not demote it, re-issue its claim speculatively on a faster model and take the first result. That satisfies 'reassigned, not deleted' while bounding tail latency. Transfers with one caveat the later literature raises: replication wastes resources, so the SpeculativeCap analogue matters.

mechanisms.name: Online load balancing on unrelated machines: Theta(log m)
mechanisms.what_it_does: For online makespan minimisation on unrelated machines the optimal deterministic competitive ratio is Theta(log m). Plain greedy is only m-competitive on unrelated machines, though it is Theta(log m) on restricted assignment and on related machines. The Omega(log m) lower bound holds even for unit-size jobs each of which can go to only 2 specific machines.
mechanisms.citation: Y. Azar, J. Naor, R. Rom, "The competitiveness of on-line assignments", SODA 1992 / Journal of Algorithms 18(2):221-237, 1995; J. Aspnes, Y. Azar, A. Fiat, S. Plotkin, O. Waarts, "On-line routing of virtual circuits with applications to load balancing and machine scheduling", JACM 44(3):486-504, 1997; lower-bound construction restated in S. Im, R. Kumar et al., "Online Load and Graph Balancing for Random Order Inputs", arXiv:2405.07949.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Assumes the full cost vector of each job is revealed on arrival, so capability is known; only the FUTURE is unknown.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Full unrelated machines.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the irreducible cost of online arrival, separate from the cost of not knowing capability: even with perfect capability knowledge you lose Theta(log m) by not knowing future claims. With 700 models that is roughly a factor 9.5, which dwarfs the 1.58 to 2 you can win by measuring capability. The priority ordering is therefore: fix arrival-order handling (batching, late binding) before investing in capability probes.

mechanisms.name: Learned weights as a compact capability prediction
mechanisms.what_it_does: For online restricted-assignment makespan, builds a prediction of dimension LINEAR in the number of machines (one weight per machine), from which O(log eta)-competitive FRACTIONAL assignments follow, where eta is prediction error. Converting fractional to integral online costs O((log log m)^3) with a nearly matching Omega-tilde(log log m) lower bound for online rounding. Later work improves the ratio and extends it from identical to unrelated machines.
mechanisms.citation: S. Lattanzi, T. Lavastida, B. Moseley, S. Vassilvitskii, "Online Scheduling via Learned Weights", SODA 2020, pp. 1859-1877, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611975994.114; S. Li, J. Xian, "Online Unrelated Machine Load Balancing with Predictions Revisited", ICML 2021, https://cse.buffalo.edu/~shil/papers/scheduling-learned-weights.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Defines exactly what the cold-start probe should OUTPUT: m numbers, one per machine, not a full m-by-n matrix and not a bracket transcript. That breaks the Omega(log m) worst-case barrier down to O(log log m) scale.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Originally restricted assignment on identical machines; the ICML 2021 follow-up extends the prediction scheme to unrelated machines.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The most concrete design instruction in this whole set: the artefact a CDSFL cold start should produce is one weight per model. That is cheap to measure, cheap to store, cheap to refresh, and is proved sufficient to beat the generic online lower bound. The founder's recursive tournament produces far more than this and is therefore over-specified for the benefit.

mechanisms.name: Computerized adaptive testing with maximum Fisher information
mechanisms.what_it_does: Estimates a latent ability from responses and selects each next item to maximise Fisher information at the current ability estimate; maximum information occurs where item difficulty matches ability, so the selected items are ones the examinee has roughly a 0.50 chance of answering correctly. Known weakness: it over-uses highly discriminating items, so exposure control and stratification are standard.
mechanisms.citation: W. J. van der Linden, C. A. W. Glas (eds.), "Computerized Adaptive Testing: Theory and Practice", Springer, 2000; W. Deng, "Stratified and Maximum Information Item Selection Procedures in Computer Adaptive Testing", Journal of Educational Measurement 47(2):202-226, 2010, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1745-3984.2010.00109.x ; LLM application: "Leveraging Computerized Adaptive Testing for Cost-effective Evaluation of Large Language Models", arXiv:2603.23506.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This IS the founder's cold-start mechanism, with 60 years of theory attached, including the optimal item-selection rule, the stopping rule, and the standard-error accounting he would otherwise have to invent.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Handles wide ability ranges by construction, which is precisely the desktop-versus-supercomputer worry restated.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers nearly intact, with the item order INVERTED. The founder proposes starting with a very hard problem. Maximum-information theory says a very hard first item is close to uninformative for everyone below the top, because almost all responses are failures and failures at an item far above ability carry little information. The correct start is a mid-difficulty item, then adapt. His recursion down to easier problems is the right shape; the entry point is wrong. The LLM-specific paper shows the whole apparatus has already been applied to ranking language models cheaply.

mechanisms.name: Dominant Resource Fairness
mechanisms.what_it_does: Generalises max-min fairness to several resource types at once by equalising each user's share of its own DOMINANT resource, the one of which it consumes the largest cluster fraction. Proved to satisfy sharing incentive (no user is better off under an equal static partition), strategy-proofness (misreporting demand cannot increase your allocation) and envy-freeness.
mechanisms.citation: A. Ghodsi, M. Zaharia, B. Hindman, A. Konwinski, S. Shenker, I. Stoica, "Dominant Resource Fairness: Fair Allocation of Multiple Resource Types", NSDI 2011; UCB/EECS-2011-18. https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2011/EECS-2011-18.html
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Requires each participant's demand vector, which is usually declared rather than measured; strategy-proofness is what makes declaration safe.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Heterogeneity of RESOURCE TYPES (CPU, GPU, memory, cost), which is the other half of the founder's question and is not covered by makespan theory at all.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The founder asks about CPU, GPU, memory, storage AND cost together. Makespan theory collapses all of that to one speed scalar. DRF is the standard answer for allocating several incommensurable resources fairly, and its strategy-proofness matters if models or seats ever self-report their own capacity. Transfers as the allocation rule for the multi-resource budget, with makespan theory handling the per-resource scheduling underneath.

open_problems: Probe cost on an unrelated-machines matrix is unsolved. Pandora's box and scheduling-with-testing price inspection, but only for JOB processing times on 1 machine or on identical machines. Speed-prediction and speed-robust results assume the capability estimate arrives free. The combined problem the founder actually has - pay a per-probe token cost to reveal individual entries of an m-by-n model-by-claim-type capability matrix, then schedule against the partially revealed matrix - does not appear in any of these literatures. This is where CDSFL has genuinely new ground, and it is a publishable problem statement.

The speed-ordered result assumes ONE global order valid for every job. For genuinely unrelated capability (one model stronger on algebra, another on combinatorics) no such order exists, and the only result that covers that case is the Omega(m) lower bound. Whether a per-claim-class order, or a small set of orders, recovers constant competitiveness is open as far as these searches reach.

Non-stationary capability. Every bandit and queueing-bandit result cited assumes fixed service rates. Model capability changes when a vendor ships an update, and the founder's roster is explicitly long-lived. No result found handles adversarial or abrupt drift in machine speeds under a makespan objective; the closest are the distortion-error bounds, which price a WRONG estimate but not a DRIFTING one.

The gap between the 3/2 hardness and the 2-approximation for R||Cmax has been open since 1990. A 2 - 1/m refinement is attributed to Shchepin and Vakhania, and a 2026 preprint gives a learning-augmented (1 + epsilon) scheme under accurate predictions that degrades to 2, but no worst-case break below 2 was found. [VERIFY:current] This should be re-checked against recent STOC/SODA/IPCO proceedings before being stated as fact.

Decentralised guarantees. The systems that satisfy the no-central-server constraint (Condor matchmaking, Sparrow, BOINC) carry measurements, not competitive ratios. The decentralised mechanism that DOES carry a proof, work stealing, loses its O(T_1/P + T_infinity) bound under heterogeneity, where Bender records that the best known approximation ratio is only O(log p). A proven peer-to-peer allocator for heterogeneous machines is not in this literature.

Correctness is absent. Every mechanism here optimises time, throughput or energy. None measures whether the answer is RIGHT. The one found that scores correctness, BOINC adaptive replication, does it by agreement between replicas, which CDSFL forbids under its no-model-voting rule. Substituting falsifier-based validation for replica agreement inside a replication-accounting scheme is unaddressed and is specific to CDSFL.

Scale-free rosters are only partially covered. 'Speed-Robust Scheduling' handles unknown speeds with m known; separate recent work handles an unknown or stochastic NUMBER of machines (arXiv:2407.15737, 'Scheduling on a Stochastic Number of Machines'; arXiv:2409.10155; and a 2025 paper on unit jobs with an unknown number of machines). Joint uncertainty in both roster size AND capability does not appear.
strongest_disagreement:
Four specific contradictions, in descending force.

1. The payoff he is chasing is bounded at roughly 1.58 to 2, and two independent literatures agree. Speed-robust scheduling, where you must group jobs before any speed is revealed, has robustness factor 2 - 1/m in general and TIGHT bounds per m approaching e/(e-1), about 1.58, when bags equal machines (Eberle, Hoeksma, Megow, Noelke, Schewior, Simon, IPCO 2021; Mathematical Programming 197(2):1009-1048, 2023; arXiv:2011.05181; Minarik, arXiv:2407.11670 generalises). Independently, in scheduling-with-testing the optimal deterministic makespan ratio is exactly the golden ratio, about 1.618, and the optimal randomized ratio is exactly 4/3 (Duerr, Erlebach, Megow, Meissner, ITCS 2018, LIPIcs 94; Albers and Eckl, WAOA 2020, arXiv:2009.13316). So a perfect, free, instantaneous cold-start measurement recovers at most about 58% to 100% in makespan over committing blind. His tournament is not free. If it consumes more than roughly 37% of the experiment's budget it is net negative by construction. That is the direct answer to "how does my idea stack up": it is chasing a bounded prize with an unbounded-cost instrument.

2. The routing policy his tiering implies is the single worst-guaranteed policy in the set. "Promote the top performers to the top tier" and then send work there is Iterative Greedy - at any time put the live job on the free machine with the largest estimated speed - and it is proved NOT competitive, with a lower bound of Omega(n) in the number of jobs (Lindermayr, Megow, Rapp, ICML 2023, PMLR 202, Appendix C). Mitzenmacher's stale-information result reaches the same conclusion from queueing theory: deterministically routing to the apparently best server significantly hurts performance once the information is stale, while a small amount of randomness restores near-perfect-information performance ("How Useful Is Old Information?", PODC 1997; IEEE TPDS 11(1):6-20, 2000). A capability ranking measured once at the start of an experiment IS stale information.

3. A tier fixed for the duration of an experiment is provably Omega(m)-competitive. Theorem 3.1 of Lindermayr, Megow and Rapp: any NON-MIGRATORY speed-oblivious algorithm has competitive ratio at least Omega(m) for total completion time, even if it is clairvoyant, the machines are related, and the speed ORDER is known. Measuring capability well does not rescue an irrevocable assignment. The same paper's Theorem 1.2 sharpens the cost: with prediction distortion mu the clairvoyant migratory bound is 8mu, but the NON-PREEMPTIVE bound is 7.216mu squared. One-shot binding squares your measurement error.

4. His cold-start item order is backwards, and his second mechanism is unstable in exactly his regime. Maximum Fisher information item selection - the 60-year-old optimal rule for adaptive ability measurement - selects items at the examinee's current estimated ability, which are items with roughly a 0.50 success probability; a very hard first item given to everyone is near-uninformative for everyone below the top, because almost all responses are failures (van der Linden and Glas, "Computerized Adaptive Testing: Theory and Practice", Springer 2000; Deng, Journal of Educational Measurement 47(2):202-226, 2010). Start mid-difficulty and adapt both ways. Separately, his knockout mechanism used as a steady-state routing policy - random pairing with no capability prior - is the speed-oblivious setting, which carries an Omega(m) lower bound even for a clairvoyant algorithm on uniform-speed machines (Lindermayr et al., Observation 1.1), and randomly sampling d servers from a heterogeneous population SHRINKS the stability region, becoming unstable well below true capacity when capacity is concentrated in a few fast servers, with the published fix being to sample within a server TYPE or to use speed-aware querying (Gardner, Jaleel, Wickeham, Doroudi, Performance Evaluation, 2020; Mukhopadhyay and Mazumdar on randomized JSQ in heterogeneous processor-sharing systems; Zhou, Shroff, Wierman, arXiv:2003.02368). A roster with 2 or 3 strong models and 60 weak ones is exactly that regime.

What the literature says he got RIGHT, and this is the useful half: the bracket's OUTPUT - a bare ordinal ranking with no magnitudes - is a sufficient statistic. Knowing only a global order of machines by unknown speed yields an 8-competitive clairvoyant algorithm and a 216-competitive non-clairvoyant algorithm on related machines, and Theta(log min{n, m}) on unrelated machines (Lindermayr, Megow, Rapp, Theorems 1.3 and 1.4). He does not need to calibrate speed, proof quality and cost into one comparable number. He needs an order, he needs migration, and he needs randomness in the routing. His two mechanisms are each half right, and the literature says which half: mechanism 2 is a good MEASUREMENT procedure and a provably bad ROUTING policy; mechanism 1 is a reasonable routing input and a badly-ordered measurement procedure.
